events.title: Rider Advocate brief: 8 claims (0 void)
events.body:
C1: This was a RydeTAXI metered trip (fare fact F6 shows a distance-charge of $28.31 computed on 20.08 km, i.e. per-km metered billing), so extra kilometres driven flow straight into what the rider paid, unlike fixed-quote services. [F6] [RD-2]
C2: GPS shows the trip ran 20.1 km against a 15.5 km optimal route (+4.6 km, +30%), and one off-route segment from 12:46 to 13:07 drove 9.70 km where the optimal route covers 5.62 km, adding 4.08 km and straying up to 1720 m from the optimal route (F1, F3) — an off-route segment under RD-1. [F1 F3] [RD-1 RD-2]
C3: No exemption applies: there were no in-app chat messages at all, so there is no rider message consenting before the segment started (F7), and the driver's own written statement 'I followed my GPS, it took me off at Paya Lebar' is a post-trip account, not prior consent (F8) — under RD-5 only the rider's own pre-segment message counts. [F7 F8] [RD-5]
C4: The driver cannot claim reasonable cause for the reroute: traffic records show no incident anywhere near the route during the trip window (F12), and the only congestion-type band on the driven road, Paya Lebar Road band 4, is far outside the band 1–2 severe-congestion range (F11); the expressways in question were flowing at band 7, 60–69 km/h (F9, F10). [F9 F10 F11 F12] [RD-4]
C5: The refund is computable on this trip's own per-km rate: the fare fact values the excess distance at $6.50, being 4.61 km × $1.4099/km (this trip's distance fare ÷ distance km) (F4, F6). [F4 F6] [RD-2]
C6: On the segment actually recorded as off-route, the excess is 4.08 km (F3), so the recoverable extra distance is 4.08 km × $1.4099/km = $5.75; the small remainder between $6.50 and $5.75 is map-matching/path noise outside the segment and is not claimed (per RD-2's bar on unsegmented differences). [F3 F4 F6] [RD-1 RD-2]
C7: The driver should additionally be referred to Ryde account review: this is an unexplained 4.08 km deviation with no traffic cause (F3, F12) and the driver already has a dispute record in the last 90 days, 0 upheld (F15), which under RD-6 supports an account flag alongside the refund. [F3 F12 F15] [RD-6]
C8: The trip took 34.0 min against an estimated 21.8 min (F2), and the driver never told the rider before leaving the optimal route — there is no chat record of any message (F7) — so the rider was charged for a route he never agreed to. [F2 F7] [RD-1 RD-5]
Weaknesses: The off-route segment's extra km as segmentised is 4.08 km (F3) while the fare tool bills the excess at 4.61 km / $6.50 (F4); if the judge accepts the larger figure the refund is $6.50, but the driver will argue the 0.53 km gap is map-matching noise not attributable to any segment, which RD-2 excludes from refund. | The rider's own profile is weak: 5 disputes in 90 days, 3 upheld (F14), which the driver can use to characterise this as a pattern of claims. | The driver's defence is that he followed his GPS-nominated route, and Ryde's own help centre lets drivers take the fastest/most efficient GPS route (A7 as reflected in RD-1's sourcing); if the judge reads the GPS route as merely 'fastest', the rider must still show no reasonable cause existed (F12 helps, but the argument is not airtight). | There is no record tying the driven segment to any named road (F3 gives only distance/time/geometry, F11 is a category-2 traffic record for Paya Lebar Road, not a routing record), so if the driver claims a specific agreed road, that part of the case would be undetermined (G13) — though here there is no consent message at all (F7), so the consent branch fails outright.
Asks: refund_partial $5.75

The refund is computable on this trip's own per-km rate: the fare fact values the excess distance at $6.50, being 4.61 km × $1.4099/km (this trip's distance fare ÷ distance km) (F4, F6).

events.title: Proposed ruling: refund_partial $5.76 (model confidence 0.90)
events.body:
This is a RydeTAXI trip billed on the meter: the total of $42.52 is built from base $3.90, distance $28.31 on 20.08 km, time $8.84, platform $1.47 [F6], so extra kilometres driven flow directly into what the rider paid and the RD-2 metered branch applies [RD-2]. The trip ran 20.1 km against a 15.5 km optimal route (+4.6 km) [F1], and the trace records exactly one measured off-route segment, 12:46–13:07, driving 9.70 km where the optimal route covers 5.62 km, adding 4.08 km [F3]; that segment is an off-route segment under RD-1 [RD-1].

No exemption applies. There is no traffic incident on the replaced stretch: AD-4(a) fails outright because no qualifying incident is recorded near the route during the trip window [F12], and the only slow road on the driven path, Paya Lebar Road, sits at speed band 4 (30–39 km/h), above the band 1–2 gate, while both expressways flowed at band 7 [F11][F9][F10]; band records alone do not exempt [RD-4].

Consent fails as well. The chat record is empty — no in-app messages between rider and driver [F7] — and the driver's "I followed my GPS, it took me off at Paya Lebar" is a post-trip written statement, not a rider message before 12:46:55 [F8]; only the rider's own pre-segment message counts, and the driver statement claiming agreement is not consent [RD-5]. RD-6 does not attach: the driver's profile shows 0 upheld route disputes in 90 days over 640 trips [F15], so the breach is not "repeated" and no account flag follows [RD-6]. The rider's own profile (5 disputes / 3 upheld [F14]) is noted but decides nothing [RD-6].

No exemption applies: there were no in-app chat messages at all, so there is no rider message consenting before the segment started (F7), and the driver's own written statement 'I followed my GPS, it took me off at Paya Lebar' is a post-trip account, not prior consent (F8) — under RD-5 only the rider's own pre-segment message counts.

The driver cannot claim reasonable cause for the reroute: traffic records show no incident anywhere near the route during the trip window (F12), and the only congestion-type band on the driven road, Paya Lebar Road band 4, is far outside the band 1–2 severe-congestion range (F11); the expressways in question were flowing at band 7, 60–69 km/h (F9, F10).
The refund is computable on this trip's own per-km rate: the fare fact values the excess distance at $6.50, being 4.61 km × $1.4099/km (this trip's distance fare ÷ distance km) (F4, F6).

On the segment actually recorded as off-route, the excess is 4.08 km (F3), so the recoverable extra distance is 4.08 km × $1.4099/km = $5.75; the small remainder between $6.50 and $5.75 is map-matching/path noise outside the segment and is not claimed (per RD-2's bar on unsegmented differences).

The driver should additionally be referred to Ryde account review: this is an unexplained 4.08 km deviation with no traffic cause (F3, F12) and the driver already has a dispute record in the last 90 days, 0 upheld (F15), which under RD-6 supports an account flag alongside the refund.

The trip took 34.0 min against an estimated 21.8 min (F2), and the driver never told the rider before leaving the optimal route — there is no chat record of any message (F7) — so the rider was charged for a route he never agreed to.

weaknesses: The off-route segment's extra km as segmentised is 4.08 km (F3) while the fare tool bills the excess at 4.61 km / $6.50 (F4); if the judge accepts the larger figure the refund is $6.50, but the driver will argue the 0.53 km gap is map-matching noise not attributable to any segment, which RD-2 excludes from refund.
The rider's own profile is weak: 5 disputes in 90 days, 3 upheld (F14), which the driver can use to characterise this as a pattern of claims.

The driver's defence is that he followed his GPS-nominated route, and Ryde's own help centre lets drivers take the fastest/most efficient GPS route (A7 as reflected in RD-1's sourcing); if the judge reads the GPS route as merely 'fastest', the rider must still show no reasonable cause existed (F12 helps, but the argument is not airtight).

There is no record tying the driven segment to any named road (F3 gives only distance/time/geometry, F11 is a category-2 traffic record for Paya Lebar Road, not a routing record), so if the driver claims a specific agreed road, that part of the case would be undetermined (G13) — though here there is no consent message at all (F7), so the consent branch fails outright.

claims.assertion: This is a RydeTAXI metered trip (total charged $42.52 built from base, distance 20.08 km, time 34.0 min), so the fare follows the meter and any route deviation is compensated by the metered-distance refund in RD-2 rather than by the fixed-quote rules; the driver does not dispute that the metered distance exceeded the estimate (F6, F1).

The GPS track shows exactly one off-route segment (12:46–13:07) adding 4.08 km, and the fare record shows excess distance billed of $6.50 computed as 4.61 km × $1.4099/km, so the refund of metered mileage units should be capped at the segment's extra_km, i.e. $5.76 (4.08 km × $1.4099/km), not the full $6.50 billed (F3, F4).

The rider's own complaint is that the driver exited the PIE at Paya Lebar, and the only traffic record on that road shows PAYA LEBAR ROAD at speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) during 12:45–13:15, i.e. ordinary slow traffic, not band 1 or 2 severe congestion, so there is no traffic evidence justifying the reroute and the deviation remains unexcused (F11).

There is no exemption on traffic grounds: the traffic data records no incidents near the route during the trip window, the expressways were flowing at band 7 (60–69 km/h), and the weather was fair with 0.0 mm rain, so no traffic incident or band 1–2 record supports the alternative route (F9, F10, F12, F13).

There is no passenger consent to the route change: the chat record contains no in-app messages at all between rider and driver, and the driver's statement that he 'followed my GPS' is a post-trip written statement and not a rider message, so no message from the rider approved the Paya Lebar deviation before the segment started at 12:46 (F7, F8).

The driver has no prior upheld route complaint — 0 upheld disputes in 90 days over 640 trips, rating 4.8 — so this appears to be an isolated incident and RD-6's 'repeated' condition is not met, and no flag_account should attach (F15).

weaknesses: The GPS excess of 4.6 km over the optimal route (+30%) and the 4.08 km off-route segment are system records that cannot be explained away; the driver's only defence, 'I followed my GPS' (F8), is a statement and RD-5 requires the rider's own pre-segment message, which does not exist (F7).

The traffic facts are unhelpful to the driver: no incident near the route (F12) and the only slow road, Paya Lebar Road at band 4 (F11), does not meet RD-4(b)'s band 1–2, so the driver has no documented reasonable cause for the reroute (F9–F13).

RD-2 refunds metered extra_km but the meter also accumulated 12.2 extra minutes (F2, F6), and the rider will argue the whole $6.50 excess and the extra time-based fare should be returned; the rider's profile shows 3 upheld route disputes in 90 days (F14), so the tribunal may view the pattern seriously even though F14 must not decide this case.

points.response: Agreed that this is a metered RydeTAXI trip billed on distance and time (F6) and that the RD-2 rail is metered mileage; that is exactly the basis of my C1/C5 and it does not weaken the refund claim — it is the mechanism by which the overcharged kilometres are returned.

The driver's own arithmetic ($5.76 on 4.08 km × $1.4099/km, F3, F4) matches mine to the cent and both sides agree the segment's extra_km, not the billed $6.50, is the recoverable figure; my claim already asks only $5.75, so the dispute on quantum is gone.

The driver concedes there is no traffic justification for the deviation (F11, F12), which is the whole of RD-4: with no exemption the 12:46–13:07 segment stands as an unexempted off-route segment under RD-1 and RD-2 requires the mileage refund.

The absence of any incident, of band 1–2 congestion and of bad weather (F9, F10, F12, F13) is entirely my point on C4, not the driver's: clear roads and fair weather were precisely the conditions in which the optimal 15.5 km route was available (F1).

The driver concedes there is no rider consent message (F7) and that his 'followed my GPS' explanation is only a post-trip statement (F8); under RD-5 consent must be the rider's own message sent before the segment starts, so the consent exemption is unavailable and the segment is unexempted.

The driver is right that RD-6's 'repeated' condition is not met — his profile shows 0 upheld disputes in 90 days (F15) — so I withdraw the account-flag limb of C7 and accept that the case turns solely on the RD-2 mileage refund.

The only variance between the two briefs is rounding ($5.75 vs $5.76 on the same 4.08 km × $1.4099/km, F3, F4); I keep my figure as it is the one I calculated, and either amount is computable from the fare fact.
points.void_reason: citation check: a rebuttal point must cite at least one fact and one clause

points.response: Conceded: the fare is metered (F6: distance $28.31 on 20.08 km), so RD-2's RydeTAXI branch applies — but that branch refunds only the unexempted segments' extra_km, nothing more.
The GPS record shows one off-route segment only, adding 4.08 km (F3), so the driver's exposure is the 4.08 km segment, not the whole 4.6 km difference from the optimal route (F1).

Agreed that no rider message exists (F7) and that F8 is a post-trip statement, so the driver does not rely on consent; likewise no consent argument can be run in reverse against a rider message that was never sent.
Conceded: no incident near the route (F12) and only band 4 on Paya Lebar Road against RD-4's band 1–2 gate (F11) means the driver has no traffic exemption, so no_action is not available.

The $6.50 figure (F4) is the fare tool's whole-trip excess-distance conversion; RD-2 requires the refund to be built from the extra_km of each unexempted segment, so F4 sets the rate of $1.4099/km (F4, F6) but not the refundable quantity.

This is the driver's own position: the recoverable amount is 4.08 km × $1.4099/km = $5.76 on the F4 rate, and the rider's own brief concedes the 0.53 km gap between F3's segment and F4's billed excess is unsegmented noise which RD-2 does not refund.
RD-6 requires a repeat finding and the rider's own profile fact shows the driver has 0 upheld disputes in 90 days across 640 trips (F15), so there is no 'repeated' breach to support a flag_account.

RD-2 makes the unexempted segment, not the trip duration, the measure of refund; the 12.2 extra minutes (F2) do not create a separate refund line, and the absence of chat (F7) is already conceded, not a second head of loss.
